contribution: The use of radiation in medicine and technology: how X-rays are produced, the contrast of an X-ray image and CT as attenuation in layers, tracers (technetium-$99\text{m}$, fluorine-18), the annihilation photons of PET $E_\gamma = m_e c^2 = 511\,\text{keV}$ and locating by coincidence with a simulation, radiotherapy from many directions, technical uses, and justification, optimisation and protection of staff.
learn: explain how the contrast of an X-ray image arises and calculate the share of radiation that gets through layers of tissue.
explain how a PET scanner locates a tracer using photons that leave in opposite directions.
justify the choices in radiotherapy and other uses of radiation in terms of safety.
prior: The intensity of gamma radiation halves in every layer of one half-value thickness $d_{1/2}$ (chapter *Ionising radiation and the body*)
Activity decreases according to the decay law $A = A_0 \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/T_{1/2}}$ (chapter *The decay law and half-life*)
Effective dose in sieverts and protection by time, distance and shielding (chapter *Radiation dose and radiation safety in Finland*)

activities.text: In a PET scan at a hospital, a small amount of radioactive sugar is injected into the patient. An hour later the patient lies inside a ring-shaped scanner, and an image appears on the screen in which a cancerous tumour glows brightly. The scanner cannot see inside the body; it only detects photons coming out of it. In another room the same hospital treats cancer with radiation that kills the cells of a tumour but spares the tissue around it.
activities.question: How can a device outside the body work out where inside the body the radiation came from, and how can radiation destroy a tumour without harming too much healthy tissue?

activities.title: Review: half-value thickness
activities.prompt: Behind a lead plate the intensity of gamma radiation is a quarter of what it is without the plate. How thick is the plate?

choices.text: Two half-value thicknesses, because the first halves the radiation and the second halves what is left.
choices.feedback: Correct. Each half-value thickness lets through half of the radiation entering it: $\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{4}$. In this chapter we use the same principle to calculate how much X-radiation gets through tissue and bone.

choices.text: Four half-value thicknesses, because each layer reduces the radiation by the same amount.
choices.feedback: A layer attenuates the same *share* of the radiation entering it, not the same amount. Behind four half-value thicknesses, $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^4 = \tfrac{1}{16}$ would get through. A quarter needs only two layers.

choices.text: Three quarters of a half-value thickness, because the plate stops three quarters of the radiation.
choices.feedback: Even one half-value thickness lets through half, so a thinner plate would let through more than half. A quarter needs two half-value thicknesses: $\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{4}$.

activities.title: Prediction 1: what a single detection tells
activities.prompt: Two opposite detectors of the PET scanner's detector ring each detect a $511\,\text{keV}$ photon almost at the same moment. What can you conclude from this single detection about the place of the annihilation?

choices.text: The annihilation happened somewhere on the line segment between the detectors, but a single detection does not tell where on the segment.
choices.feedback: The simulation supports this: every coincidence draws a line segment between two detectors, and the segments cross the whole body. The photons leave in nearly opposite directions, so the source is on the segment or very close to it. When the difference in arrival times is not measured, as in the model, a single detection does not reveal the place on the segment. The place becomes clear only from the intersections of many segments.

choices.text: The annihilation happened exactly at the midpoint of the segment between the detectors, because the photons arrived at the same time.
choices.feedback: In the simulation the segments pass through the tumour even when the tumour is not in the middle of the segment. The photons arrive at the detectors within a few nanoseconds, and the coincidence detection treats them as simultaneous even if one travelled a longer distance: light travels about $30\,\text{cm}$ in a nanosecond. A modern scanner measures the time difference with an accuracy of about $0.3\,\text{ns}$, which narrows the source to a stretch of a few centimetres on the segment, but not to a single point. The image is still formed from many segments.

choices.text: The annihilation happened near one of the detectors, because a photon is produced where it is detected.
choices.feedback: In the simulation the photons are produced inside the body at the annihilation point and fly from there to the detectors. A detector only detects the photon. Because the photons leave in opposite directions, the source is somewhere on the line segment between the detectors.

activities.title: Prediction 2: how many detections are needed
activities.prompt: A patient has a tumour in the lung where more tracer has accumulated than in the rest of the body, but there is also tracer elsewhere in the body. How many coincidences are needed for the brightest spot of the image to fall on the tumour?

choices.text: Tens, because only some of the segments pass through the tumour and the other segments intersect each other at random places.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: after $10$ coincidences the brightest spot was about $18\,\text{cm}$ from the tumour, after $20$ it was $4.0\,\text{cm}$, after $50$ only $1.4\,\text{cm}$ and after $200$ it was $0\,\text{cm}$ away. Only about a quarter of the segments passed through the tumour. With small values of $N$ the result varies by chance: with a different random order, the brightest spot could fall on the tumour already at $20$ or only at about $100$ coincidences.

choices.text: Two are enough, because two segments intersect at one point.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: even after $20$ coincidences the brightest spot was $4.0\,\text{cm}$ from the tumour. There is tracer in the whole body, so most of the segments do not pass through the tumour, and their random intersections drown the tumour until there are tens of segments.

choices.text: One is enough, because a segment always passes through the place where the most tracer has accumulated.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: only about a quarter of the segments passed through the tumour, and after $10$ coincidences the brightest spot was about $18\,\text{cm}$ from the tumour. A segment starts from the place where a single nucleus happened to decay, and that can be anywhere in the body.

activities.title: Prediction 3: radiotherapy from many directions
activities.prompt: In radiotherapy a tumour deep in the body is often irradiated from five or more directions, even though the radiation could reach the tumour from just one direction. Why?

reveal.pending: The feedback opens when you have read the Radiotherapy section of the Theory summary.

choices.text: Only the tumour receives the dose of all the beams, and healthy tissue along each beam receives only one beam.
choices.feedback: Correct. With five beams, each giving $0.40\,\text{Gy}$ to the tumour, the tumour receives $5 \cdot 0.40\,\text{Gy} = 2.0\,\text{Gy}$, but healthy tissue along each beam receives only about $0.40\,\text{Gy}$. From one direction the same $2.0\,\text{Gy}$ would pass entirely through the same healthy tissue.

choices.text: The radiation does not pass through the tumour, so it has to be directed at it from all sides for the whole tumour to receive a dose.
choices.feedback: The high-energy X-radiation of radiotherapy passes through the whole body, including the tumour. Many directions are needed because the beams intersect only at the tumour: the tumour receives the dose of all the beams, healthy tissue only that of one beam.

choices.text: From many directions the treatment is finished faster, because each beam needs less time.
choices.feedback: Treatment time is not the reason: the beams are usually given one after another, so the total time does not get shorter. The reason is sparing healthy tissue: the tumour receives the dose of all the beams, but the healthy tissue along each beam receives the dose of only one beam.

activities.text: A cross-section of a patient is inside the detector ring of a PET scanner. Collect coincidences and follow how the image on the right is built from the segments and where its brightest spot is.
activities.howto: *Start collecting* collects coincidences, and *Stop* stops the collection. *Coincidences* sets the number $N$ of collected coincidences directly between $0$ and $2000$. *Patient* chooses whether the body has one tumour, two tumours or no tumour; the tumour is not drawn in the body, but it is found in the image. *Detection* switches between coincidence detection and counting single photons. On the left, two orange photons fly in opposite directions from the annihilation point, the detectors that were hit flash, and a line segment is drawn between them. On the right is the image calculated from the segments: the more segments pass through a pixel, the brighter it is. *Speed* changes only the pace of the collection.
activities.model: The tracer is spread evenly through the body, and $25\,\%$ of the annihilations come from the tumour ($20\,\%$ from each of two tumours). The radius of the tumour is about $1\,\text{cm}$, so its tracer concentration is tens of times that of the rest of the body. The photons leave in exactly opposite directions in a random direction in the plane, and the body neither attenuates nor scatters them. The distance travelled by the positron and random coincidences are not included. The ring is two-dimensional and detects every photon pair. The model does not use the difference in the photons' arrival times. A real scanner collects tens of millions of coincidences. The readings are values of the model, not measurements.
activities.calc: The annihilations are always drawn in the same order, so the same $N$ always gives the same image. A different drawing order would give a different result with small values of $N$, because the random intersections of the segments vary. The image is a grid of $41 \cdot 41$ points with a spacing of $1\,\text{cm}$. Each segment adds one hit to every pixel whose distance from the segment is less than $0.6\,\text{cm}$. The brightest spot is the point with the most hits, and the reading *distance from the tumour* is its distance from the centre of the nearest tumour. *Lines through the tumour* is the share of the segments that pass within $1.0\,\text{cm}$ of the centre of the tumour. In the detection of single photons, only one photon of each pair is detected, so only the detector is known and not the segment.

activities.title: Experiment 1: how many segments are needed
activities.intro: Test predictions 1 and 2. The patient has one tumour, and the detection is coincidence. Change only the number of coincidences $N$ and record the distance of the brightest spot of the image from the tumour for at least $N = 10$, $20$, $50$ and $200$. At the same time, look at what kinds of segments are drawn in the ring.

activities.title: Conclusion: how PET locates
activities.prompt: Write on the basis of your table: What does a single coincidence tell about the place of the source? How did the distance of the brightest spot from the tumour change as more coincidences accumulated, and why? What does this mean for the patient's dose?
activities.model: A single coincidence tells that the annihilation happened somewhere on the line segment between two detectors, because the photons leave in opposite directions; the model does not use the difference in arrival times. With the values of the model, the brightest spot of the image was about $18\,\text{cm}$ from the tumour after $10$ coincidences and $4.0\,\text{cm}$ after $20$, but after $50$ only $1.4\,\text{cm}$ and after $200$ it was $0\,\text{cm}$ away. With large values of $N$, about a quarter of the segments passed through the tumour, because there is tracer in the whole body. With few segments the random intersections are as bright as the tumour, and only after tens of segments do the segments that pass through the tumour stand out. With small values of $N$ the result varies by chance. A good image therefore needs many decays, that is, a sufficient activity. That is optimisation: the activity is chosen large enough for the image to answer the question, but no larger.
criteria: I say that a single coincidence limits the source to the line segment between two detectors, and I justify it with the photons leaving in opposite directions.
Using the values of the model, I say that the brightest spot fell on the tumour only when there were tens of coincidences, and that with small numbers the result varies by chance.
I explain that only some of the segments pass through the tumour, because there is tracer elsewhere in the body too.
I connect the required number of coincidences to the activity and the patient's dose.
I call the numbers of the simulation values of the model, not measurements.

activities.title: Investigate: at what energy an X-ray image is taken
activities.text:
The table gives the half-value thickness $d_{1/2}$ of soft tissue and bone at three X-ray photon energies. The last column tells how large a share of the radiation gets through a $20\,\text{cm}$ layer of soft tissue, which corresponds to the body of an adult.

| Energy | $d_{1/2}$ tissue | $d_{1/2}$ bone | $20\,\text{cm}$ of tissue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $30\,\text{keV}$ | $1.8\,\text{cm}$ | $0.27\,\text{cm}$ | $0.05\,\%$ |
| $60\,\text{keV}$ | $3.4\,\text{cm}$ | $1.1\,\text{cm}$ | $1.6\,\%$ |
| $100\,\text{keV}$ | $4.1\,\text{cm}$ | $1.9\,\text{cm}$ | $3.3\,\%$ |
activities.source_note: calculated from the attenuation coefficients of the NIST XCOM database for a narrow beam (water as soft tissue, compact bone as bone), rounded

question.prompt: At which energy do bone and soft tissue differ the most, and why is an X-ray image of the body nevertheless taken at a higher energy?

choices.text: The difference is greatest at $30\,\text{keV}$, but then only $0.05\,\%$ gets through the body, so almost all of the radiation stays in the patient.
choices.feedback: Correct. The ratio of the half-value thicknesses is $1.8 : 0.27 \approx 7$ at $30\,\text{keV}$ and only $4.1 : 1.9 \approx 2$ at $100\,\text{keV}$, so the contrast is best at low energy. However, low-energy radiation hardly gets through a thick body: it is absorbed in the patient, gives a dose and produces no image. The lowest energy is used for thin targets, such as in breast imaging.

choices.text: The difference is greatest at $100\,\text{keV}$, because high-energy radiation passes through bone better than low-energy radiation.
choices.feedback: High-energy radiation passes better through both bone and soft tissue, so the difference between them gets smaller: the ratio of the half-value thicknesses is $4.1 : 1.9 \approx 2$ at $100\,\text{keV}$ and $1.8 : 0.27 \approx 7$ at $30\,\text{keV}$. A higher energy is used so that the radiation gets through the body.

choices.text: The difference is the same at all energies, because bone is always equally denser than soft tissue.
choices.feedback: The ratio of the densities stays the same, but attenuation also depends on the energy of the photon and on the number of electrons in the atoms. The ratio of the half-value thicknesses is about $7$ at $30\,\text{keV}$ and about $2$ at $100\,\text{keV}$, so the difference gets smaller as the energy grows.

activities.title: Return to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the values of the model and the theory. Then return to the opening question: how does a PET scanner work out the place of the tracer, and how does radiotherapy spare healthy tissue?

activities.title: Find the mistake
activities.prompt: A beam passes through $5.0\,\text{cm}$ of soft tissue and $3.0\,\text{cm}$ of bone. A student calculates: “$0.36$ gets through the soft tissue and $0.15$ through the bone, so altogether $0.36 + 0.15 = 0.51$, about half of the radiation, gets through.” Where is the mistake?

choices.text: The shares must be multiplied: through the bone gets $0.15$ of what got through the soft tissue, that is, $0.36 \cdot 0.15 \approx 0.054$.
choices.feedback: Correct. Only the share $0.36$ that got through the soft tissue enters the bone, and the bone lets through the share $0.15$ of that. So $0.36 \cdot 0.15 \approx 0.054$, about $5\,\%$, gets through. The sum cannot be right: through two layers cannot get more than through either of them alone.

choices.text: The thicknesses of the layers must be added first and one half-value thickness used for the whole $8.0\,\text{cm}$.
choices.feedback: Soft tissue and bone have different half-value thicknesses, so one value cannot be used. Each layer is calculated with its own half-value thickness, and the shares that got through are multiplied: $0.36 \cdot 0.15 \approx 0.054$.

choices.text: The shares must be divided, because bone attenuates more: $0.36 : 0.15 = 2.4$.
choices.feedback: A share cannot be over $1$, because a layer does not add radiation. The bone lets through the share $0.15$ of the radiation that got through the soft tissue, so the shares are multiplied: $0.36 \cdot 0.15 \approx 0.054$.

activities.title: Apply: the journey of a tracer to the hospital
activities.prompt: The tracer for a PET scan is made in a cyclotron in another city at $8.30$, and the patient is injected with $300\,\text{MBq}$ at $11.00$. The half-life of fluorine-18 is $110\,\text{min}$. How large an activity must the patient's dose have when it is made at $8.30$? Give the answer in megabecquerels.
hints: How long is it from the production to the injection? How many half-lives is that?
The decay law $A = A_0 \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/T_{1/2}}$ gives the activity $A$ at the time of the injection. Here $A$ is known, and $A_0$ is asked.
The time is $150\,\text{min}$, that is, $\tfrac{150}{110} = 1.36$ half-lives, so $A_0 = 300\,\text{MBq} \cdot 2^{1.36}$.

mistakes.feedback: You calculated how much of $300\,\text{MBq}$ is left after $150\,\text{min}$. Here $300\,\text{MBq}$ is needed *at the end*, so at the start the activity must be larger: $A_0 = A \cdot 2^{t/T_{1/2}}$.
You took only one half-life into account. The time is $150\,\text{min}$, which is $\tfrac{150}{110} = 1.36$ half-lives, so the factor is $2^{1.36} \approx 2.57$.
The time and the half-life must be in the same unit. The time that passed is $2.5\,\text{h} = 150\,\text{min}$, not $2.5\,\text{min}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** the activity needed at the time of the injection $A = 300\,\text{MBq}$, production at $8.30$, injection at $11.00$, half-life of fluorine-18 $T_{1/2} = 110\,\text{min}$

**Asked:** the activity $A_0$ at the time of production in megabecquerels

**Principle:** Activity is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei, so it decreases according to the decay law: every half-life halves it. No substance is added or removed during the journey, so the law describes the whole transport.

**Formula:** $A = A_0 \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/T_{1/2}}$, so $A_0 = A \cdot 2^{t/T_{1/2}}$

**Conversions:** The time that passed is $t = 11.00 - 8.30 = 2\,\text{h}\ 30\,\text{min} = 2 \cdot 60\,\text{min} + 30\,\text{min} = 150\,\text{min}$, in the same unit as the half-life.

**Substitution:** $A_0 = 300\,\text{MBq} \cdot 2^{150\,\text{min} / 110\,\text{min}} = 300\,\text{MBq} \cdot 2^{1.3636} = 300\,\text{MBq} \cdot 2.5733 = 772.0\,\text{MBq}$

**Answer:** $770\,\text{MBq}$, two significant figures, because the dose $300\,\text{MBq}$ is given with two or three significant figures.

**Reasonableness:** A little over one half-life passes, and clearly less than two, so the factor must be between $2$ and $4$: $2.57$ is. After one half-life, $386\,\text{MBq}$ would be left of $772\,\text{MBq}$, and the next $40\,\text{min}$ reduce it to $300\,\text{MBq}$. Because of the short half-life, the cyclotron has to be within a few hours' journey.

activities.text: Practise at three levels. Level 1 tasks use one equation, level 2 tasks convert units or combine two equations, and level 3 requires reasoning.

activities.title: 1. Concept
activities.prompt: Why is technetium-$99\text{m}$, which emits gamma radiation of $140\,\text{keV}$ and has a half-life of $6.01\,\text{h}$, suitable as a tracer for radionuclide imaging?

choices.text: Gamma radiation escapes from the body to the detector, and a half-life of a few hours is enough for imaging but soon makes the activity small.
choices.feedback: Correct. The image is formed outside the body, so the radiation must escape from the body, and gamma radiation ionises sparsely along its way. After a day only about $6\,\%$ of the activity is left, so the patient's dose stays small.

choices.text: Gamma radiation stops in the organ where the tracer has accumulated, and a long half-life gives time to image the patient many times.
choices.feedback: If the radiation stopped in the organ, a detector outside the body would not detect it and no image would be formed. Gamma radiation escapes from the body. A half-life of $6.01\,\text{h}$ is short: after a day only about $6\,\%$ of the activity is left.

choices.text: Gamma radiation ionises more densely than alpha radiation, so even a small activity shows up clearly in the image.
choices.feedback: Alpha radiation ionises most densely, and that is exactly why it stops in tissue within the distance of a few cells and does not escape from the body. Gamma radiation ionises sparsely, so it reaches the detector and gives the patient a small dose.

activities.title: 2. Calculate the frequency of an annihilation photon
activities.prompt: The energy of a photon produced in annihilation is $511\,\text{keV}$. How large is the frequency of the photon? Give the answer in hertz.
hints: Which equation connects the energy and the frequency of a photon (chapter *The photoelectric effect and the photon*)?

mistakes.feedback: The energy must be converted from electronvolts to joules before dividing by the Planck constant: $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** the energy of the photon $E = 511\,\text{keV}$, the Planck constant $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$ and $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$

**Asked:** the frequency $f$ of the photon in hertz

**Principle:** The energy of a photon is proportional to its frequency, $E = hf$ (chapter *The photoelectric effect and the photon*). An annihilation photon is a quantum of electromagnetic radiation like a photon of visible light, so the same equation holds.

**Formula:** $E = hf$, so $f = \dfrac{E}{h}$

**Conversions:** $E = 511\,\text{keV} = 511 \cdot 10^{3}\,\text{eV} = 511 \cdot 10^{3} \cdot 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J} = 8.186 \cdot 10^{-14}\,\text{J}$

**Substitution:** $f = \dfrac{8.186 \cdot 10^{-14}\,\text{J}}{6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}} = 1.2355 \cdot 10^{20}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{s}}$

**Answer:** $1.24 \cdot 10^{20}\,\text{Hz}$, three significant figures like the energy $511\,\text{keV}$.

**Reasonableness:** The frequency of visible light is about $5 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$ and the energy of a photon about $2\,\text{eV}$. The energy is now about $2.6 \cdot 10^{5}$ times as large, so the frequency must be that many times larger: $5 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz} \cdot 2.6 \cdot 10^{5} \approx 1.3 \cdot 10^{20}\,\text{Hz}$, as in the result.

activities.title: 3. Explain and transfer
activities.prompt: A PET patient has just been injected with a fluorine-18 tracer and waits an hour before the scan. Explain why the nurse keeps away from the patient during this time, although the nurse can stand next to a patient who has had an X-ray right after the examination. Name two other ways of keeping the nurse's dose small, and explain why the syringe shield for a PET tracer must be thicker than for technetium-$99\text{m}$.
activities.model: The tracer is in the patient's body, and every decay of fluorine-18 produces two $511\,\text{keV}$ photons that escape from the body. The patient is therefore a radiation source until the tracer has decayed or left the body. X-radiation, on the other hand, is produced only while the tube is on, and nothing radioactive stays in the patient. The nurse reduces the dose with distance, because the dose rate decreases with the square of the distance, and with time, because the dose is the dose rate times the time spent: the nurse does only what is necessary at the patient's side, and quickly. In addition, the tracer is handled behind a lead or tungsten shield, and the nurse wears a dosimeter. Photons of $511\,\text{keV}$ pass through lead much more easily than photons of $140\,\text{keV}$: the half-value thickness of lead is about $3.9\,\text{mm}$ instead of $0.26\,\text{mm}$, so about $15$ times as thick a shield is needed for the same attenuation.
criteria: I explain that a patient who has received a tracer emits radiation until the tracer has decayed or left the body, but X-radiation stops when the tube is switched off.
I justify the effect of distance and time: the dose rate decreases with the square of the distance, and the dose grows with the time spent.
I mention shielding, such as a shielded syringe or a protective wall, or a dosimeter.
I justify the thicker shield with the half-value thickness of lead for $511\,\text{keV}$ photons being much larger than for $140\,\text{keV}$ photons.
